indicators.flag:
The use of a private investment vehicle that is based offshore to purchase CRE and that
includes PEPs or other foreign nationals (particularly family members or close associates of
sanctioned Russian elites and their proxies) as investors.
indicators.rationale: A bank can flag offshore investment-vehicle counterparties, but tying them to PEP/sanctioned-elite proxies needs beneficial-ownership enrichment it only partially holds.

indicators.flag:
When asked questions about the ultimate beneficial owners or controllers of a legal entity or
arrangement, customers decline to provide information.
indicators.rationale: Refusal-to-provide-UBO is a standard CDD onboarding/EDD checkpoint already captured in KYC workflows at a mid-size bank.

indicators.flag:
Multiple limited liability companies, corporations, partnerships, or trusts are involved in a
transaction with ties to sanctioned Russian elites and their proxies, and the entities have slight
name variations.
indicators.rationale: Slight-name-variation clusters of counterparty entities transacting together are detectable from the bank's own counterparty-name and wire data via fuzzy-match — a defensible build-now transaction pattern.

build_logic.logic: Cluster counterparty legal entities (LLC/corp/partnership/trust) by normalized-name edit-distance and shared address/signatory; alert when ≥3 slight-name-variant entities co-transact in a single CRE-coded financing within the window.
build_logic.source: counterparty master + wire/ACH ledger + CRE loan-coding
build_logic.route: Tier-1 alert → enhanced-due-diligence analyst review gate

indicators.flag:
The use of legal entities or arrangements, such as trusts, to purchase CRE that involves
friends, associates, family members, or others with a close connection to sanctioned Russian
elites and their proxies.
indicators.rationale: Establishing a close personal connection between an entity's parties and sanctioned elites requires external sanctions-network/relationship attribution the bank does not hold.

indicators.flag:
Ownership of CRE through legal entities in multiple jurisdictions (often involving a trust
based outside the United States) without a clear business purpose.
indicators.rationale: Multi-jurisdiction ownership layering is visible only with beneficial-ownership/corporate-registry enrichment beyond core transaction data.

indicators.flag:
Transfers of assets from a PEP or Russian elite to a family member, business associate, or
associated trust in close temporal proximity to a legal event such as an arrest or an OFAC
designation.
indicators.rationale: Transfer-timing relative to an OFAC designation is computable, but identifying the originator as a PEP/elite and the recipient relationship needs external designation-feed and relationship enrichment.

indicators.flag:
Implementation of legal instruments (e.g., deeds of exclusion) that are intended to transfer
an interest in CRE from a PEP or Russian elite to a family member, business associate, or
associated trust following a legal event such as an arrest or an OFAC designation of that
person.
indicators.rationale: Deed-of-exclusion and CRE-title instruments live in external asset/property registries the bank does not ingest.

indicators.flag:
Private investment funds or other companies that submit revised ownership disclosures to
financial institutions showing sanctioned individuals or PEPs that previously owned more
than 50 percent of a fund changing their ownership to less than 50 percent.
indicators.rationale: Revised ownership-disclosure deltas across the 50 percent threshold are in the bank's KYC-refresh records; enhancing existing disclosure-change monitoring catches them.

indicators.flag:
There is limited discernable business value in the CRE investment or the investment is outside
of the client’s normal business operations.
indicators.rationale: Out-of-profile / no-apparent-business-purpose activity is already part of transaction-monitoring scenarios; enhancing the client-profile model sharpens it.
